lead: A power reading alone does not show how good an engine is. Judge it with the fuel and air that produced the power, measured while load is steady. Fuel is timed or weighed; air is metered by orifice, venturi or hot wire. Their mass ratio is air-fuel ratio; air flow against swept volume gives volumetric efficiency. Every test bed, type-approval run and workshop diagnosis starts here.
prereq: You need 5.1 for power and efficiency, and Unit 2 for fuel supply.

sections.h3: Fuel flow: burette, balance and meters

blocks.text: Fuel flow is a mass flow in kg/h, because combustion needs a fixed air mass per fuel mass. Three methods are common.
Volumetric method: the engine draws fuel from a glass burette with two marks setting volume V. A stopwatch times the fall between marks.

blocks.where: ṁf is fuel mass flow in kg/h; V is burette volume in L; ρ is fuel density in kg/L at fuel temperature (about 0.83 diesel, 0.74 petrol); t is time in s; 3600 converts s to h.

items: Fill the burette above the top mark while the engine runs from the main tank.
Turn the three-way cock so the engine draws only from the burette.
Start the stopwatch at the top mark; stop at the bottom mark; note t.
Repeat three times and average; correct ρ to fuel temperature.

blocks.text: The three-way cock lets the engine run from the tank while the burette refills, so filling time is never timed.
Small volume and short time increase error. A 50 mL burette read to ±1 mL is ±2 %; 25 s timed to ±0.2 s is ±0.8 %. A 5 s test makes timing error ±4 %. Use the largest volume and longest steady time.
Gravimetric method weighs fuel from a can on a balance and clocks the time to lose a set mass, say 100 g. No density is needed; accuracy is better, so it calibrates others.

items: Rotameter: float rises with flow; cheap, steady flow only, needs density correction.
Turbine meter: rotor speed gives volume as pulses.
Coriolis meter: measures mass directly; best accuracy, highest cost.
Gas fuels: gas meter gives volume at meter pressure and temperature; convert with ρ = p/(R T).

sections.h3: Air flow: air box, orifice and hot wire

blocks.text: Air is harder to meter because intake flow pulses every stroke, so a settling volume smooths it.

Air box: a large tank the engine breathes from, with a sharp-edged orifice open to the room. The box damps pulses; the orifice sees steady flow. A U-tube manometer reads pressure drop Δp across the orifice, usually as water column h in mm.

blocks.where: ṁa is air mass flow in kg/s; C_d is discharge coefficient (about 0.6 sharp-edged orifice, 0.98 venturi); A is orifice area in m²; ρ is air density in kg/m³; Δp is pressure drop in Pa, equal to 9.81 × h for h in mm of water.

blocks.text: Air density comes from the test room: ρ = p ÷ (R T), where p is absolute room pressure in Pa, T is room temperature in K, and R = 287 J/(kg·K) for air. A hot Chennai afternoon changes ρ by several per cent, moving air flow and volumetric efficiency.

A venturi meter uses the same relation with higher C_d and smaller permanent loss; flow benches use it. A hot-wire anemometer heats a thin wire and measures current to keep it hot; flow cools the wire, so current reads velocity. It responds fast enough for pulsating intake and in-cylinder work.
Engine-as-compressor method: motor the engine with fuel cut off, collect and measure pumped air, for example in a gas meter. This gives breathing alone, without combustion disturbing flow.
Both flows must be in the same units before dividing. With ṁa and ṁf in kg/s, air-fuel ratio is AFR = ṁa ÷ ṁf, always by mass, never by volume.
Stoichiometric values are about 14.7 for petrol and 14.5 for diesel. A light-load diesel may run at 30 or more; a petrol engine at full power runs near 12.
Volumetric efficiency compares air actually trapped per cycle with the mass that would fill swept volume at intake density.

blocks.where: η_vol is volumetric efficiency; ṁa is measured air flow in kg/s; ρ_a is intake air density in kg/m³; V_s is total swept volume in m³; N is engine speed in rev/min. For a four-stroke, ÷ 2 gives one intake stroke in two revolutions; a two-stroke uses (N ÷ 60) with no halving.

blocks.text: Values near 85 to 95 % are normal for a good four-stroke at full throttle. Far below points to blocked filter, bad cam or hot intake; see 5.6.

figure.caption: Fuel flow and air flow are measured separately: their mass ratio is the air-fuel ratio, and air flow against ideal swept-volume flow is volumetric efficiency. Measured 0.052 kg/s is below ideal 0.059 kg/s.

spec.title: Two flows, one ratio
spec.aria: Block diagram: burette timing gives fuel mass flow in kg/h, air box gives air mass flow in kg/s, their ratio is the air-fuel ratio, and air flow against the ideal swept-volume flow gives volumetric efficiency.

examples.question: A four-cylinder four-stroke engine of 2.0 L swept volume runs at 3000 rpm. Air box orifice gives 0.052 kg/s; intake air density is 1.18 kg/m³. A burette test uses 50 mL diesel of density 830 kg/m³ in 25 s. Find fuel flow in kg/h and kg/s, air-fuel ratio by mass, and volumetric efficiency.
steps: Fuel mass: m = V × ρ = 0.050 L × 0.83 kg/L = 0.0415 kg. (830 kg/m³ = 0.83 kg/L.)
Ideal air flow for four-stroke: ṁa,ideal = ρ_a × V_s × (N ÷ 60) ÷ 2 = 1.18 × 2.0 × 10⁻³ × (3000 ÷ 60) ÷ 2.
examples.answer: Fuel flow 5.98 kg/h (1.66 × 10⁻³ kg/s), air-fuel ratio 31.3 by mass, volumetric efficiency 88.1 %.
examples.check:
V = 0.050
rho = 0.83
t = 25.0
ma = 0.052
rho_a = 1.18
Vs = 2.0e-3
N = 3000.0

m = V * rho
mf_h = m * 3600 / t
mf_s = mf_h / 3600
afr = ma / mf_s
ideal = rho_a * Vs * (N / 60) / 2
eta = 100 * ma / ideal
print(round(mf_h, 2))
print(round(mf_s, 5))
print(round(afr, 1))
print(round(ideal, 3))
print(round(eta, 1))

traps: Quoting AFR by volume. AFR is always a mass ratio; a volume ratio near 31 is meaningless.
Skipping air density correction. ρ = p ÷ (R T) changes AFR and volumetric efficiency by several per cent.
Timing burette refill. The three-way cock must switch supply so the engine never drinks during filling.
Forgetting ÷ 2 for a four-stroke in ideal air flow; it doubles swept volume and halves efficiency.
Mixing units: mL with L, mm water with Pa, kg/h with kg/s. Convert and check answer size.

quiz.q: Define volumetric efficiency of an IC engine.
quiz.a: The ratio of air mass actually trapped per cycle to the mass that would fill total swept volume at intake air density, usually as a percentage.

quiz.q: Why is a three-way cock used in the burette method?
quiz.a: It lets the engine run from the tank while the burette fills, then switches the engine to draw only from the burette, so filling time is not timed.

quiz.q: Why is the gravimetric method more accurate than the volumetric method?
quiz.a: It measures mass directly on a balance, so no density value is needed and no volume reading error enters. The volumetric method depends on burette reading and fuel density.

quiz.q: A 100 mL burette of petrol of density 0.74 kg/L is emptied in 40 s at steady load. Find the fuel flow in kg/h.
An air box orifice has area 1.2 × 10⁻³ m² and C_d = 0.62. The manometer reads 50 mm of water and air density is 1.18 kg/m³. Find the air flow in kg/s.
Why is a large air box placed before the orifice?
quiz.a: Intake flow pulses with each stroke. The box damps pulses, so the orifice sees nearly steady flow and the orifice equation stays valid.

quiz.q: Air flow falls by 10 % while fuel flow and speed stay the same. What happens to air-fuel ratio, power and exhaust?
quiz.a: AFR falls about 10 %, so mixture is richer. Power changes little in a diesel but smoke and CO rise as oxygen becomes short; a petrol engine may give slightly more power but higher fuel use and emissions.

quiz.q: Two engines of the same swept volume run at the same speed; one shows 92 % volumetric efficiency and the other 78 %. Give two likely physical causes and one consequence.
quiz.a: Causes: restricted intake (blocked filter, small port) or hot low-density intake charge. Consequence: less air per cycle, so less power for the same fuel and a richer mixture.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production cars use hot-film mass air flow sensors; the ECU computes injection from them, so the same physics runs in real time. Research beds use Coriolis meters and fast analyzers cycle by cycle to study cylinder-to-cylinder maldistribution. Hydrogen and CNG engines need gas meters and density corrections to standard conditions.
